title: Shvetaketu and the word that points
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a proud son, a cup of salt water, and the Gayatri's first word
carry: hindus point to brahman as tat: that
tomorrow: of Savitr: is that the sun, or something behind the sun?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king became a sage, and the Gayatri asks one thing: stir our minds. Today, its very first word.

A text arrives with no photo and no link, just two words: that one. So you scroll up, hunting for whatever that is. The Gayatri opens the same way. Its first word is tat, that. And the thing it points at doesn't show up next. Two more words go by, the line ends, and only at the start of the next line does the noun arrive. Why would a prayer begin by pointing?
screen: `A TEXT THAT JUST SAYS: THAT ONE.`
`TAT: THAT.` → `THE NOUN IS A LINE AWAY.`

segments.voice: First the reader's answer. Tat is the neuter form of that, and the next neuter noun is bhargo, radiance, a line away. Varenyam matches too, like teammates in the same jersey. So the grammar says: that radiance. But Hindus care about this small word for a bigger reason. Tat is how the tradition points at God. In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu comes home at twenty-four after twelve years of study, proud, sure he knows it all. His father, Uddalaka, asks one question: did you learn the thing by which the unheard becomes heard? He hadn't. So the father teaches with what's at hand. Put this salt in water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning. The salt is gone; the boy can't find it. Sip from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle. Salty. From the bottom. Salty. You can't see it, but it's in every drop. That fine thing in everything is the real, the self, he says, and then the line Hindus have repeated ever since: tat tvam asi. That, you are. This is Brahman, the one reality, and it can't be held up like a cup on a table, so the teachers point: that. The Gita gives three words for Brahman, Om tat sat, and tat is the middle one. In the Gayatri, the grammar only points to the radiance. Many teachers hear the same reach in it: the verse begins by turning toward what's bigger than the one saying it.
screen: `TAT POINTS TO BHARGO, A LINE AWAY.` · `SALT IN WATER: IN EVERY DROP.` · `TAT TVAM ASI: THAT, YOU ARE.` · `OM TAT SAT.` · then, large: `GOD IS POINTED AT, NOT HELD.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on the farthest thing you can see: a window, a doorway, the far wall. Silently call it only that, without naming it. If you have a glass of water near you, take one slow sip and remember the salt you couldn't see. Stay facing toward that while the time runs.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: tat, that, the word that waits a line for its noun, and the word Hindus point to Brahman with.
screen: `THE GAYATRI AND THE PEACE CHANTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line to take with you: Hindus point to Brahman as tat: that, because it is in everything. That, you are. That's day fifteen hundred.

screen: `DAY 1500 COUNTS.` → `HINDUS POINT TO BRAHMAN AS TAT: THAT.` → `TOMORROW: THE SUN, OR BEHIND THE SUN?`

howItsDone: Teachers who explain the Gayatri word by word often begin with tat and show how it waits for bhargo, the radiance. Hindus also use tat for Brahman, as in Om tat sat and the Chandogya's tat tvam asi.

fork.setup: Sam asks why Hindus would call God 'that' instead of a name. which answer comes from the Upanishad?
options: it's rude in Sanskrit to say God's name out loud.
Brahman is in everything, like salt in water, so you point instead of holding it up.
Sanskrit had no word for God.
fork.reveal: Uddalaka showed his son the salt he couldn't see but could taste in every drop: tat tvam asi, that, you are.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: tat, that, the first word of the Gayatri verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first word is a filler sound, like a warm-up.
what it means: tat, that, points at the radiance; and Hindus point to Brahman with the same word.
what a scholar hears: tat is a neuter demonstrative agreeing with neuter bhargas and varenyam; tat tvam asi and Om tat sat use the same pronoun for Brahman.
recall: we hold in mind: the people's verb
the king who became the Gayatri's seer

notes: Gayatri word by word: tat. Grammar stated: tat as neuter nominative/accusative singular of the demonstrative, agreeing with neuter bhargas (bhargo by sandhi) and vareṇyam. Confirm wording for learners.
'The first word' means of RV 3.62.10 itself, not counting Om bhur bhuvah svah, which day 1265 explained sits outside the verse.
The Chandogya link is only that the same word appears; the script makes no claim that teachers read the Gayatri's tat through tat tvam asi.
